planting.note: Divide and transplant clumps into humus-rich, well-drained shade soil in spring after new growth begins.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to partial shade, sheltered from harsh winter wind. New wiry black-stemmed fronds emerge bronze-pink in spring and mature to blue-green, persisting through winter in milder climates. Top-dress annually with leaf mold or compost and keep evenly moist but never waterlogged. Old tattered fronds can be cut back in late winter before new growth flushes.

planting.note: Transplant bare-root divisions or rooted stem sections into moist, humus-rich soil beneath a dense forest canopy in fall or early spring.

directions: Site in deep, consistently moist shade beneath conifers, mimicking its native Pacific Northwest old-growth understory habitat. Wear gloves when handling, as stems and leaf undersides bear dense sharp spines. Bark and root bark are traditionally harvested from mature stems in fall for medicinal preparations, similar in use to Panax ginseng. Grows slowly and spreads by layering sprawling stems that root where they touch moist duff; leave leaf litter in place as mulch rather than clearing it away.
sources: University of Alaska Fairbanks Cooperative Extension

planting.note: Transplant rooted runner segments into cool, moist, acidic duff-rich soil under a closed forest canopy in spring.

directions: Grow as a low trailing groundcover in cool, consistently moist, acidic soil under dense conifer or mixed forest shade, replicating its native old-growth Pacific Northwest habitat. Thin trailing stems root at the nodes and spread slowly across mossy duff, bearing small three-to-five-lobed strawberry-like leaves. Solitary white flowers give way to small raspberry-red aggregate fruits prized by foragers but rarely produced in cultivation outside cool, humid coastal climates. Avoid heat, drought, and disturbed or compacted soil, which the species will not tolerate.
